\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{booktabs}

\title{Two-Year Soil Moisture Monitoring on a Terraced Hillslope\\Under Monsoon and Irrigation Forcing}
\author{S.~Bekele, H.~Okafor, and T.~Marek}
\date{August 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
This paper reports on two years of continuous soil moisture
monitoring on a terraced hillslope farm growing maize and vegetables
under monsoon rainfall and supplemental irrigation. A dense array of
capacitance probes, tensionmeters, and weather sensors recorded more
than four hundred million readings between 2024 and 2026. We describe
the field campaign, present the observed moisture dynamics and their
seasonal variation, and show that irrigation-induced changes in topsoil
water content reach 40\%, exceeding the changes attributable to
rainfall alone by a factor of three. The dataset is released to support
benchmarking of irrigation-scheduling algorithms under realistic
monsoon variability.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Terraced hillslopes are among the most intensively managed agricultural
landscapes, and the case for instrumenting them is straightforward: the
cost of a failed season dwarfs the cost of a monitoring network, and
early detection of water stress can raise yields by double digits. Yet
the promise of irrigation scheduling based on soil moisture sensing
remains only partly realised, largely because monsoon variability masks
the subtle signatures of stress in the quantities that most algorithms
track.

The confounding role of rainfall has been recognised for decades, but
quantitative models of the rainfall--moisture relationship are still
largely site-specific, and the community lacks long, openly available
records in which weather and irrigation events are logged with the same
care as the soil response itself. The campaign described here was
designed from the outset to close this gap: every soil sensor is paired
with weather channels, and the data pipeline preserves raw readings
alongside the derived moisture products.

The contributions of the paper are threefold. First, we document a
two-year monitoring campaign on a working terraced farm in full
operational detail. Second, we quantify the seasonal and daily
variation of moisture at six depths and attribute it to specific
drivers. Third, we release the complete dataset together with the
processing chain, so that scheduling methods can be benchmarked against
realistic, uncurated variability.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 describes
the site and the sensors. Section 3 presents the field campaign in
detail. Section 4 reports the observed moisture dynamics and their
drivers, Section 5 discusses implications for irrigation scheduling,
and Section 6 concludes.

\section{Site and Sensors}
The monitored site is a 12-hectare terraced hillslope farm with maize
on the upper terraces and vegetables below, cultivated for two decades.
The soils are silty clay loams over weathered bedrock, and the terrace
bunds date from a 1998 consolidation programme.

The instrumentation was specified jointly by the farm cooperative and
the research team, with the explicit goal that weather channels should
match soil channels in number and in quality. The full probe layout is
presented in Section 3.2. Power and telemetry budgeting follows
Section 3.3. The data acquisition system samples all channels on a
common clock, and the timing error between the most distant nodes is
kept below one second by a weekly synchronisation pass.

Three design decisions shaped the installation. First, all sensors were
selected for a five-year service life with in-place calibration,
because terrace access for maintenance is restricted to the
post-harvest window. Second, the irrigation flow is monitored
indirectly through pressure transducers on each lateral, avoiding the
cost of inline meters. Third, the raw readings are retained rather than
only hourly summaries, which roughly doubles the storage cost but
preserves the option of reprocessing with future algorithms.

\section{Field Campaign}
This section describes the two-year campaign in operational detail.

\subsection{Campaign Timeline}
The installation began in April 2024 with the ridge probes and
proceeded terrace by terrace, so that partial coverage was available
from June 2024 onward. Full coverage was reached in November 2024, and
the analysis period used in this paper runs from December 2024 to
December 2026, omitting the commissioning phase. Planned outages for
maintenance totalled eleven days over the two years, and unplanned
outages, mostly caused by a failing gateway at the pump house, totalled
a further six days.

\subsection{Probe Layout}
The probe array comprises 36 capacitance probes on the terraces, 12 on
the bunds, and 44 low-cost resistive pickups in the vegetable beds,
together with 36 tensionmeters installed at six depth profiles. The
terrace probes are spaced at 17~m along the contours, which resolves
the wetting front with a spatial aliasing limit well above the scale of
the irrigation laterals. Water table depth below the lower terraces is
tracked by two pressure loggers in existing wells, providing an
independent slow channel that anchors the profile integration of the
capacitance records.

The probe positions were chosen by a representativeness criterion
evaluated on the soil map of the farm, subject to the constraint that
all terrace sensors be reachable from the existing bund paths. The bed
pickups are buried two hand-widths below the ridge tops, deep enough to
avoid cultivation damage and shallow enough to be serviced from a small
hand auger without disturbing the crop rows.

\subsection{Telemetry and Power}
All nodes sample at 15-minute intervals with 16-bit resolution, and the
gateways timestamp each packet against the synchronised clock. Data are
transmitted over a LoRa mesh to the pump house, where they are written
to redundant storage in one-day segments. A watchdog process verifies
segment completeness every hour and pages the on-call technician when
any node misses three consecutive checks. The moisture derivation runs
nightly on the previous day's data using an automated calibration
pipeline, and its results are archived with full provenance metadata.

\subsection{Soil Sampling}
The soil sampling programme visits every terrace block at planting and
at harvest, taking auger cores at the six depth profiles for
gravimetric calibration of the capacitance probes. The cores inside the
profiles are paired at the topsoil and subsoil horizons, so that the
vertical drying gradient that drives the daily uptake cycle can be
resolved directly rather than inferred from surface readings alone.
Grain moisture records are quality-controlled against the cooperative's
separate storage sensors, and the two systems agree within 0.4\% on the
weekly means.

\subsection{Quality Screening}
Every channel passes through an automated screening chain that flags
spikes, dropouts, drift, and flatline faults against channel-specific
thresholds learned during commissioning. On average 1.8\% of
channel-days are flagged each month, concentrated in the resistive
pickups after lightning storms and in the pressure loggers during heavy
rain. Flagged segments are never discarded silently: they are excluded
from the moisture derivation but retained in the archive with the flag
metadata, so that users of the dataset can apply their own trade-off
between coverage and quality.

\section{Results}
The moisture records at six depths range from near-saturation after
monsoon bursts to the wilting point in the dry season, and all profiles
are tracked successfully on more than 97\% of the days in the analysis
period. The drying rates identified by the calibration pipeline average
0.6\% per day for the topsoil and 0.9\% per day for the subsoil
profiles, in line with values reported for comparable terraces.

The dominant source of moisture variability is irrigation. The topsoil
water content varies by 40\% between the driest and wettest weeks of
the record, and a hysteresis loop against rainfall collapses onto a
single curve when plotted against the irrigation volume instead. As
Section 3.2 explains, the probes are seated in augered holes, which
rules out installation artefacts as the origin of the loop and supports
the interpretation in terms of lateral scheduling and terrace storage.

A weekly periodicity is visible in the derived drying rates of the
topsoil profiles, with weekend values about 15\% lower than weekday
values. We attribute this to the changed irrigation rota rather than to
any soil cause: the share of sprinkler events falls on weekends, and
the lighter, more uniform drip events wet the beds more coherently,
which biases the calibration pipeline toward lower apparent drying.

Rainfall is the second driver but a much weaker one in the irrigated
season: the moisture difference between the driest nights and the
heaviest monsoon bursts is below 6\% for the topsoil profiles. The
calibration follows the sampling protocol of Section 3.4, and after
calibration the residual variability of the topsoil record drops from
40\% to 4\%, which defines the noise floor against which any scheduling
index must be evaluated on this site. The flagging follows the
screening chain of Section 3.5, and flagged days account for most of
the remaining residual.

\section{Discussion}
The results quantify, for this farm, the well-known warning that
calibration against gravimetric sampling is not an optional refinement
but a prerequisite for scheduling: an uncalibrated controller would
raise seasonal false alarms with an amplitude ten times the residual
noise floor. The released dataset, with its paired weather channels, is
intended to let other groups test their calibration and scheduling
methods without the multi-year negotiation that usually precedes access
to farm monitoring data.

Two limitations deserve emphasis. The record covers two full monsoons
and is therefore informative about seasonal but not about decadal
variability, and the farm suffered no crop failure during the period,
so the dataset benchmarks false-alarm behaviour but not failure
detection power.

\section{Conclusion}
We have documented a two-year soil moisture monitoring campaign on a
terraced hillslope farm, from the probe layout and telemetry chain to
the derived moisture dynamics and their drivers. The headline numbers
are stark: irrigation moves the topsoil water content by 40\%, rainfall
by less than 6\%, and calibration reduces the residual to 4\%. The
complete dataset and processing chain are released to the community.
Future work will use the record to develop transferable calibration
models and to test scheduling algorithms under controlled injection of
synthetic drought stress.
\end{document}

dialogue.persona: 农场传感器项目的博士后，中文交流，急性子，需求一次说清但会中途变卦；变卦时先否定上一轮再给新指令，不解释太多。
dialogue.hiddenGoal: 终态：Field Campaign 章内小节顺序为 Campaign Timeline、Probe Layout、Soil Sampling、Quality Screening、Telemetry and Power——即相对初始顺序只把 Telemetry and Power 整节（标题带正文）挪到本章最后，其余四节原位；5 个小节一个不少，小节正文一字不改。正文四处手写节号引用同步：两处 Probe Layout 引用保持 Section 3.2；Site and Sensors 里 telemetry budgeting 那句改成指向 Section 3.5；Results 里 sampling protocol 改成指向 Section 3.3；Results 里 screening chain 改成指向 Section 3.4。剧本：第 1 轮让 agent 对调 Probe Layout 和 Soil Sampling 并修正引用。agent 做完后第 2 轮用户改主意：“对调撤了吧，恢复到原来顺序；然后把 Telemetry and Power 整节挪到这章最后，节号引用跟着改对。”若 agent 还没做完对调，同样话术（“先别对调了……”）。后续轮次：用户抽查 Telemetry 是否在章末、sampling protocol 是否指向 3.3；有错指出让返工，全对确认结束。用户知识边界：记得五个小节标题和大致内容，背不下逐字正文，验收靠翻文件看节的位置和引用数字。
